newsitem.title: USA: Missing funds witness may return to U.S. - ABC.
newsitem.headline: Missing funds witness may return to U.S. - ABC.

text.p: A former Little Rock restaurant owner and large contributor to the Democratic Party said on Sunday said he may be enticed to return to the United States from China as early as this week.
Charles Yah Lin Trie, in an interview with ABC-TV's "World News Tonight," said his lawyers have been urging him to come back and make a deal with the Justice Department.
Trie, who has been living in Beijing for the past few weeks, said his lawyers told him he would probably be indicted for fund raising and other financial violations, ABC said.

"I've got nothing to hide," Trie said in his first on-camera television interview since leaving the United States. Earlier this month, Trie talked to NBC in Shanghai, but refused to let the interview be filmed.

Republicans have cited Trie's departure from the United States and the refusal of other key players to testify in asking Attorney General Janet Reno to recommend an independent probe of the matter, but she has refused so far.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott on Sunday stopped short of asking for Reno's resignation, but said he was considering other possible actions against the nation's top law enforcement official for allegedly blocking probes that could embarrass President Bill Clinton.
In Sunday's interview, Trie dismissed Republican allegations that he engaged in espionage for the Chinese government, saying, "This kind of thing totally is false."
He gave no details on the deal his lawyers were working out with the Justice Department.

Trie, living in Beijing, has refused to testify before a U.S. Senate committee investigating campaign finance scandals. The Democratic National Committee has returned the $645,000 donated or raised by Trie from Asian-American sources,
Trie told ABC that DNC officials never asked him where the money came from nor explained U.S. fund-raising laws.

The committee is investigating how foreign money was illegally raised and spent in the 1996 elections and whether U.S. security was compromised by individuals who may have shared secret information with foreign business interests.

Separately, the White House denied a report in Sunday's Los Angeles Times quoting Southern California entrepreneur and big Democratic Party donor Johnny Chung as saying that he gave a $50,000 check to the first lady's chief of staff on White House grounds in 1995 in direct response to solicitations by Hillary Rodham Clinton's aides.

Chung, contradicting the administration's version of the incident, said he was seeking VIP treatment for visiting Chinese executives when he was asked to help the first lady defray the cost of White House Christmas receptions billed to the Democratic National Committee.
Chung told the Times he realised such special treatment hinged on his willingness to make a political contribution.
But White House Counsel Lanny Davis said the allegations were "untrue" and Chung's own attorney had denied in March that his client made a donation in exchange for favours.
Chung, a Taiwan-born businessman, contributed $366,000 to the DNC between mid-1994 and last November's election.

He has denied Republican allegations that he may have funnelled Chinese government money to the DNC, but has refused to cooperate with campaign fund raising investigators unless granted immunity from prosecution.

Margaret Williams, the first lady's former chief of staff who has acknowledged accepting a $50,000 check from Chung at the White House, is the subject of a pending inquiry by the agency charged with enforcing the Hatch Act, which prohibits federal employees from soliciting contributions, as well as by congressional panels probing campaign finance abuses.
The article also mentioned another White House aide, Evan Ryan.

"Neither Maggie Wiliams or Evan Ryan solicited a contribution from Mr. Chung nor promised him favours in return for a contribution," Davis said. The White House has insisted that Williams played "a completely passive" role in relaying an unsolicited check for $50,000 to the DNC.
